# MetaSEM

All codes are from the author of the [package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/metaSEM/vignettes/Examples.html)

Custom comparison functions

```{r}
compare_models_wls <- function(model1, model2){
    library(tidyverse)
  # Extract names of model1 and model2 as character strings
  model1_name <- deparse(substitute(model1))
  model2_name <- deparse(substitute(model2))
  
  fit_measures_combined <- inner_join(as.data.frame(summary(model1)$stat) %>% rename(!!model1_name := Value) %>% rownames_to_column(),
                                      as.data.frame(summary(model2)$stat) %>% rename(!!model2_name := Value)%>% rownames_to_column(), 
                                      by = "rowname") %>% 
    mutate(decsion = "",
           understanding = '') %>% 
    mutate(
      decsion = case_when(
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "Chi-square of target model" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "Chi-square of independence model" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "RMSEA" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "SRMR" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "TLI" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "CFI" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "AIC" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] < .[[3]] & rowname == "BIC" ~ model1_name, 
        
        
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "Chi-square of target model" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "Chi-square of independence model" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "RMSEA" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "SRMR" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "TLI" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "CFI" ~ model1_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "AIC" ~ model2_name, 
        .[[2]] > .[[3]] & rowname == "BIC" ~ model2_name, 
        TRUE ~ decsion
      )
    ) %>% 
    
    mutate(
      understanding = case_when(
        rowname == "Chi-square of target model" ~ "This measures the difference between the observed data and the model-predicted data. A small chi-square value indicates a good fit. However, the chi-square statistic is sensitive to sample size and may not be a reliable fit measure for large samples.", 
        rowname == "Chi-square of independence model" ~ "This measures the difference between the observed data and the model-predicted data. A small chi-square value indicates a good fit. However, the chi-square statistic is sensitive to sample size and may not be a reliable fit measure for large samples.", 
        rowname == "RMSEA" ~ "This measures the fit of the model to the data in terms of the difference between the observed and predicted covariances. A value of RMSEA less than 0.08 is generally considered a good fit.", 
        rowname == "SRMR" ~ "This measures the fit of the model in terms of the difference between the observed and predicted covariances, standardized by the degrees of freedom. A SRMR value less than 0.08 is generally considered a good fit.", 
        rowname == "TLI" ~ "a goodness of fit measure for structural equation models (SEM). It compares the fit of the model being tested to the fit of a null model that assumes all variables are independent. A TLI value of 1 indicates perfect fit, and values close to 1 indicate good fit.", 
        rowname == "CFI" ~ "This measures the fit of the model relative to a null model (a model with no relationships between the variables). A CFI value of greater than 0.95 is generally considered a good fit.", 
        rowname == "AIC" ~ "a measure of the relative quality of statistical models. It is based on the likelihood function, which measures how well a model fits the data. The AIC is defined as the negative log-likelihood of the model, plus a penalty term for the number of parameters in the model. A lower AIC value indicates a better fit.", 
        rowname == "BIC" ~ "The BIC is similar to the AIC, but it has a stronger penalty for the number of parameters in the model. As a result, the BIC tends to favor models with fewer parameters, even if those models have a slightly worse fit to the data. A lower BIC value indicates a better fit.", 
        TRUE ~ understanding
      )
    ) %>% 
    
    mutate_at(vars(2,3), round, 2)
  return(fit_measures_combined)
}

```

## Univariate meta-analysis

### Random-effects model

```{r}
## Load the library
library(metaSEM)

## Try to use more than one cores
mxOption(NULL, 'Number of Threads', parallel::detectCores()-4)

## Show the first few studies of the data set
head(Becker83)
## Random-effects meta-analysis with ML
summary( meta(y=di, v=vi, data=Becker83) )
```

### Fixed-effects model

```{r}
## Fixed-effects meta-analysis by fixing the heterogeneity variance at 0
summary( meta(y=di, v=vi, data=Becker83, RE.constraints=0) )
```

### Mixed-effects meta analysis

```{r}
## Mixed-effects meta-analysis with "log(items)" as the predictor
summary( meta(y=di, v=vi, x=log(items), data=Becker83) ) 
```

## Missing covariates with FIML

```{r}
## Sample data from Tenenbaum and Leaper (2002, Table 1).
Tenenbaum02 <- Tenenbaum02[, c("r", "v", "Offspring_age", "Year_pub")]

## Set seed for reproducibility
set.seed(1234567)

## Let's drop 40% in Offspring_age
missing_per <- 0.4

## MCAR
index <- round(nrow(Tenenbaum02)*missing_per)
index <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), times=c(index, nrow(Tenenbaum02)-index))
index <- sample(index)
my.MCAR <- Tenenbaum02
my.MCAR[index, "Offspring_age"] <- NA
my.MCAR$Offspring_age <- scale(my.MCAR$Offspring_age, scale=FALSE)
my.MCAR$Year_pub <- scale(my.MCAR$Year_pub, scale=FALSE)

my.MCAR
```

No need to do anything else, the model automatically handles missing data

```{r}
## y: effect size
## v: sampling variance
## x: covariate
## av: auxiliary variable
fit <- metaFIML(y=r, v=v, x=Offspring_age, av=Year_pub, data=my.MCAR)
summary(fit)
```

## Multivariate Meta-analysis

### Random-effects model

```{r}
## Show the data set
Berkey98

## Multivariate meta-analysis with a random-effects model
mult1 <- meta(y=cbind(PD, AL), v=cbind(var_PD, cov_PD_AL, var_AL), data=Berkey98) 

summary(mult1)

## Plot the effect sizes
plot(mult1)
```

```{r}
## Plot the effect sizes with the forest plots
## Load the library for forest plots 
library("metafor")

## Create extra panels for the forest plots
plot(mult1, diag.panel=TRUE, main="Multivariate meta-analysis",
axis.label=c("PD", "AL"))

## Forest plot for PD
forest( rma(yi=PD, vi=var_PD, data=Berkey98) )
title("Forest plot of PD")

## Forest plot for AL
forest( rma(yi=AL, vi=var_AL, data=Berkey98) )
title("Forest plot of AL")
```

### Fixed-effects model

```{r}
## Fixed-effects meta-analysis by fixiing the heterogeneity variance component at 
## a 2x2 matrix of 0.
mult1_fixed <- summary( meta(y=cbind(PD, AL), v=cbind(var_PD, cov_PD_AL, var_AL), data=Berkey98,
              RE.constraints=matrix(0, nrow=2, ncol=2)) )
```

### Mixed-effects model

```{r}
## Multivariate meta-analysis with "publication year-1979" as a predictor 
summary( meta(y=cbind(PD, AL), v=cbind(var_PD, cov_PD_AL, var_AL), data=Berkey98,
              x=scale(pub_year, center=1979)) )
```

## Three-level meta-analysis

This section discusses the benefits of using SEM to conduct three-level meta-analyses, including the ability to compare models and construct LBCI, as well as how to use REML and FIML to handle missing covariates.

Basically three-level means that you use some grouping variable to be clusters

### Comparison between two- and three-level models

```{r}
#### Cooper et al. (2003)
library("metaSEM")
data(Cooper03)
head(Cooper03)
```

## Two-stage Structural Equation Modeling (TSSEM)

```{r}
#### Load the metaSEM library for TSSEM
library(metaSEM)
  
#### Inspect the data for inspection
head(Digman97$data)
head(Digman97$n)
```

### Fixed-effects TSSEM

#### Stage 1

```{r}
## Fixed-effects model: Stage 1 analysis
fixed1 <- tssem1(Cov=Digman97$data, n=Digman97$n, method="FEM")
summary(fixed1)
```

To conduct a fixed-effects TSSEM, we may specify method=FEM argument (the default method) in calling the tssem1() function. The results are stored in an object named fixed1. It can be displayed by the summary() command. The χ2(130,N=4,496)=1,499.73,p\<.001χ2(130,N=4,496)=1,499.73,p\<.001, CFI=0.6825, RMSEA=0.1812 and SRMR=0.1750. Based on the test statistic and the goodness-of-fit indices, the assumption of homogeneity of correlation matrices was rejected.

When the assumption of homogeneity of correlation matrices is rejected in the first stage of two-stage structural equation modeling, it means that the correlations between the latent variables are not the same across groups. This can be problematic because it means that the model may not be accurately representing the relationships between the latent variables.

There are a few options for addressing this issue:

1.  Consider collecting more data to increase the sample size and improve the precision of the estimates.
2.  Use a different estimation technique that does not rely on the assumption of homogeneity of correlation matrices, such as the mean and covariance structure (MACS) model.
3.  Use a multigroup structural equation model, which allows for the examination of differences in the relationships between latent variables across groups.
4.  Consider collecting data from a different sample that is more homogenous with respect to the latent variables in question.
5.  If the assumption of homogeneity of correlation matrices is only slightly violated, you may be able to proceed with the analysis and interpret the results cautiously, keeping in mind the potential impact of the violation on the results.

```{r}
coef(fixed1)
```

The pooled correlation matrix (the parameter estimates) can be extracted by the use of the coef() command.

#### Stage 2

```{r}
model1 <- "## Factor loadings
           Alpha =~ A+C+ES
           Beta =~ E+I
           ## Factor correlation
           Alpha ~~ Beta"

plot(model1)
```

As an illustration, I continued to fit the structural model based on the pooled correlation matrix. We may specify the two-factor model with the RAM formulation. An alternative and easier way to specify the model is to use lavann's syntax.

```{r}
RAM1 <- lavaan2RAM(model1, obs.variables=c("A","C","ES","E","I"),
                   A.notation="on", S.notation="with")
RAM1
```

Since we are conducting a correlation structure analysis, the error variances are not free parameters. The chi-square test statistic of the Stage 2 analysis was χ2(4,N=4,496)=65.45,p\<.001χ2(4,N=4,496)=65.45,p\<.001, CFI=0.9802, RMSEA=0.0585 and SRMR=0.0284.

```{r}
fixed2 <- tssem2(fixed1, RAM=RAM1, intervals="LB",
                 model.name="TSSEM2 Digman97")
summary(fixed2)
plot(fixed2)
```

### Fixed-effects TSSEM with cluster

#### Stage 1

There are 4 types of sample characteristics in the original cluster. We may group them into either younger or older sample.

```{r}
#### Fixed-effects TSSEM with several clusters
#### Create a variable for different cluster
#### Younger participants: Children and Adolescents
#### Older participants: others
clusters <- ifelse(Digman97$cluster %in% c("Children","Adolescents"),
                   yes="Younger participants", no="Older participants")
  
#### Show the clusters
clusters
```

We may conduct a fixed-effects model by specifying the cluster=clusters argument. Fixed-effects TSSEM will be conducted according to the labels in the clusters. The goodness-of-fit indices of the Stage 1 analysis for the older and younger participants were χ2(80,N=3,658)=823.88,p\<.001χ2(80,N=3,658)=823.88,p\<.001, CFI=0.7437, RMSEA=0.1513 and SRMR=0.1528, and χ2(40,N=838)=344.18,p\<.001χ2(40,N=838)=344.18,p\<.001, CFI=0.7845, RMSEA=0.2131 and SRMR=0.1508, respectively.

```{r}
## Example of Fixed-effects TSSEM with several clusters
cluster1 <- tssem1(Digman97$data, Digman97$n, method="FEM", 
                   cluster=clusters)
summary(cluster1)
```

The pooled correlation matrix for each cluster can be extracted by the use of the coef() command.

```{r}
coef(cluster1)
```

#### Stage 2

The goodness-of-fit indices of the Stage 2 analysis for the older and younger participants were χ2(4,N=3,658)=21.92,p\<.001χ2(4,N=3,658)=21.92,p\<.001, CFI=0.9921, RMSEA=0.0350 and SRMR=0.0160, and χ2(4,N=838)=144.87,p\<.001χ2(4,N=838)=144.87,p\<.001, CFI=0.9427, RMSEA=0.2051 and SRMR=0.1051, respectively.

```{r}
cluster2 <- tssem2(cluster1, RAM=RAM1, intervals.type="z")
#### Please note that the estimates for the younger participants are problematic.
summary(cluster2)
```

```{r}
library(semPlot)

## Convert the model to semPlotModel object with 2 plots
my.plots <- lapply(X=cluster2, FUN=meta2semPlot, latNames=c("Alpha","Beta"))

## Setup two plots
layout(t(1:2))
semPaths(my.plots[[1]], whatLabels="est", nCharNodes=10, color="green")
title("Younger") 
semPaths(my.plots[[2]], whatLabels="est", nCharNodes=10, color="yellow")
title("Older")

```

### Random-effects TSSEM

#### Stage 1

Since there is not enough data to estimate the full variance component of the random effects, I estimate the variance component with a diagonal matrix in the RE.type="Diag" argument. The range of I2I2 indices, the percentage of total variance that can be explained by the between study effect, are from .84 to .95.

```{r}
#### Random-effects TSSEM with random effects on the diagonals
random1 <- tssem1(Digman97$data, Digman97$n, method="REM", RE.type="Diag")
summary(random1)
```

The pooled correlation coefficients (fixed effects) and the variance components (the random effects) can be extracted by the use of the coef() command via the select argument.

```{r}
## Fixed effects
coef(random1, select="fixed")

## Random effects
coef(random1, select="random")
```

#### Stage 2

The steps are exactly the same as those in the fixed-effects model. The chi-square test statistic of the Stage 2 analysis was χ2(4,N=4,496)=8.51,p\<.001χ2(4,N=4,496)=8.51,p\<.001, CFI=0.9911, RMSEA=0.0158 and SRMR=0.0463.

```{r}
random2 <- tssem2(random1, RAM=RAM1, intervals="LB")
summary(random2)

## Plot the parameter estimates
plot(random2, color="green")
```

### Comparison between fixed and random effects

```{r}
compare_models_wls(fixed2, random2)
```
